analysis.title: AI debt unlikely to rattle bond markets
key_insights: Five major hyperscalers (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle) plan USD 4-6tn of data centre investment in 2025-30, with a large part funded from public and private debt markets.

Hyperscaler capex is planned at USD 710bn in 2026 (up almost 60% yoy) and USD 1.1tn in 2027 (up more than 50% yoy), implying about USD 1tn a year in 2028-30. Free cash flow is expected to turn negative from next year, so external funding is required.

Capex at more than 3% of US GDP exceeds the share spent on US railroads (1865-1890), electrification, the interstate highway system and telecom/internet (1996-2003). Those booms involved excess capex and ended in market crashes, though the infrastructure stayed in use.

Almost 40% of investment needs, up to USD 2.4tn, are expected to be funded through the bond market. Organic cash flows and new equity should cover 25%, and alternative capital (project finance, private equity, private credit) another 25%.

Hyperscaler leverage stays low on balance sheet, except for Oracle (highly leveraged but with contractual backing), because of off-balance-sheet SPV and private credit structures. These structures are complex and opaque and can disguise the extent of leverage in the system.

In the Hyperion (Project Beignet) structure, Blue Owl-affiliated funds own 80% and Meta 20% of the joint venture, which issued about USD 27.3bn of secured notes. This structure limits Meta's direct borrowing but does not remove its economic exposure or contingent liabilities.

About USD 46bn of equity investment and cash has been deployed across hyperscalers, AI labs, chipmakers and neoclouds, against roughly USD 879bn of multi-year purchase commitments. Commitments are not automatically leverage, but they are an indicator of financial commitment relative to deployed capital.

Circular relationships among hyperscalers, chip producers and AI labs may make the boom self-reinforcing on exaggerated assumptions and obscure the level of end demand. IT equipment is financed mostly with internal funds while real estate and power are financed with external asset-backed debt, which can mean higher effective leverage at the asset level.
Hyperscalers placed USD 192bn of bonds this year versus USD 93bn last year, and about USD 60bn equivalent in euros in 2025-26. The report sees scope for another EUR 5-10bn of euro issuance this year.

Hyperscaler issuance is small relative to outstanding markets: a USD 10bn issue is 0.03% of the UST market (USD 32tn) and 0.16% of the USD IG non-financial market (USD 6.3tn). A EUR 10bn issue is 0.08% of EGBs (EUR 12tn) and 0.5% of euro IG non-financial corporates (EUR 1.8tn).

The six euro-denominated hyperscaler issues since 2025 (four Alphabet, one Amazon, one Meta, EUR 6bn to EUR 14bn each) hurt the technology sector's relative performance in European corporate bonds. A EUR 6bn issue is almost 7% of the sector's outstanding bonds.

Issuance will gradually raise the technology sector's weight in credit indices (currently about 5%) and its average duration. Index-focused investors will need to hold more tech, tech and AI-related spread moves and rating changes will matter more for the index, and the index becomes slightly more rate-sensitive.

Impact on European government bonds should be limited because hyperscalers have largely avoided the 5-, 7-, 10-, 11- and 15-year maturities governments use. The report does not exclude some competition with less liquid EGBs or SSA bonds.

Medium- to long-term risks include overinvestment, credit quality deterioration and possible defaults. Other risks are AI model efficiency gains reducing infrastructure needs, difficulty forecasting demand, and greater hyperscaler regulation after the US midterm elections.

sector_views.rationale: Euro hyperscaler issuance has weighed on tech bond relative performance. Its weight and duration in credit indices will rise, making the index more sensitive to AI-related spread moves and rates.

risk_factors: Excessive hyperscaler investment leading to credit quality deterioration and defaults.
Opaque off-balance-sheet SPV and private credit funding structures that can disguise leverage.
Circular financing among hyperscalers, AI labs, chipmakers and neoclouds, with USD 879bn of purchase commitments against USD 46bn deployed.
AI model efficiency gains and demand uncertainty reducing future infrastructure needs.
Greater regulation of hyperscalers after the US midterm elections.
Larger or more frequent hyperscaler bond issuance could affect broader bond markets.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers have strong ratings (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft AA-area, Oracle BBB), low balance sheet leverage and large bond markets that can absorb issuance. Issuance is small relative to outstanding volumes and avoids government maturity brackets.
tension_points.bear_case: Opaque off-balance-sheet SPV and private credit leverage, circular financing (USD 879bn of commitments versus USD 46bn deployed), and possible overinvestment could deteriorate credit quality and lead to defaults.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Free cash flow turning negative from next year and AI demand, utilisation or pricing disappointing against the contractual commitments.

theme_stances.key_argument: High hyperscaler capex will reshape but not disrupt fixed income markets in the short term, while medium- to long-term credit risks loom.
theme_stances.evidence: High hyperscaler capex will reshape but not disrupt fixed income markets in the short term.
